title: Code Red: the Business Impact of Code Quality
summary: Adam Tornhill summarises the Code Red study: technical debt wastes a large share of developer time, unhealthy code has far more defects and slower, less predictable changes, and hotspots show where to pay debt down.

assertions.quote: the average company wastes 23-42% of developers' time due to technical debt and bad code in general

verdicts.note: Besker et al. surveys report roughly a quarter of time self-reported as wasted, but the figures are self-reported and vary widely.

Respondents reporting high technical debt were 1.6 times less productive and the highest performers were 1.4 times more likely to have low technical debt; the survey measures a productivity drag, not a fraction of working time.

The paper's own measurement is per-file (issues in Alert code take 124% longer, Warning 78%) rather than a share of total time; in related work it relays Besker et al.'s longitudinal self-reports of 23% of time wasted on TD and Stripe's 42% figure, which are secondary citations here.

assertions.quote: Red code has, on average, 15 times more defects than a healthy codebase.

verdicts.note: The Code Red paper on 39 codebases is correlational and from the vendor of the code-health metric; the direction matches other complexity-defect studies.

Across 30,737 files in 39 proprietary codebases, Alert (low Code Health) files had 15x the Jira defects of Healthy files and issues took 124% (about 2.2x) longer on average, so 'many times more defects' holds but 'several times longer' overstates the average time effect; observational, CodeScene-customer sample, vendor-authored, causality direction acknowledged as open.

Functions scored less readable were more likely to carry FindBugs warnings, change next release, and be touched by bug-fix commits (f-measure 0.62-0.65, precision about 0.9, recall about 0.5) across 15 open-source Java projects; supports the defect half of the claim for low readability but measures nothing about time to change.

assertions.quote: Adding a feature to healthy code seems to be a predictable process. Not so in unhealthy red code

verdicts.note: Task-time variance in red code is reported in one vendor study; independent replication is lacking.

The maximum Time-in-Development per file was 9x longer in Alert code than Healthy code (large effect, Cohen's d 0.96) and already 2x in Warning code, with much higher variance, which the authors read as lower predictability of task completion; correlational, single tool vendor's customer base.

assertions.quote: Unmitigated technical debt with high interest fuel developer attrition.

verdicts.note: Graziotin and others link bad code to frustration and lower productivity; attrition effects are anecdotal.

In DORA's model technical debt reduces productivity, productivity improves work recovery, and work recovery reduces burnout, so the link to well-being is indirect through two steps; attrition is not measured.

assertions.quote: focus on development hotspots to remediate high-interest debt first

verdicts.note: Change-frequency weighting is a sensible proxy supported by defect-prediction research, but comparative outcome data is limited to vendor case studies.

assertions.quote: the shorter your cycle times for deployment, the fewer production failures
code is an abstract concept that isn't accessible to non-technical stakeholders

verdicts.note: The motivation section relays that the business impact of code quality is vague, managers in a 15-organisation study would not fund refactoring because benefits were unclear, there are no code-quality KPIs comparable to financial ones, and only 10% of 1,831 surveyed said their business manager managed TD; all cited from other studies rather than measured here.
